section.title: Advanced KeystoneJS
section.description: Seventeen UI/UX lessons that turn Keystone into a component platform: relationships, list filters, virtual fields, GraphQL query states, responsive summaries, editable charts, draft/publish, and a learner-published showcase rendered by Keystone.

lessons.title: Components, two worlds
lessons.outcome: Tell the difference between a Keystone Admin UI component and a public showcase component, and choose where each one should live.
mental_model: **Keystone has two surfaces.** The Admin UI is a React/Next app you can extend with custom pages and field views; the public showcase is a separate React surface that reads Keystone through GraphQL.
**GraphQL is the boundary.** Keystone stores content and exposes typed queries and mutations; your components decide how that data becomes UI.
**Server data, client interaction.** Fetch Keystone data on the server where possible and keep only interactive controls on the client.

lab.title: Build the bridge card
lab.brief: Start with a plain card. Give it a clear hierarchy, one action, and enough space to breathe. Then publish it to the showcase.
checklist: The headline is the first thing you read
The body copy supports the headline
There is one obvious action
The action is reachable with the keyboard
The card still works at 360px wide
hints: Use the eyebrow for context, not a second headline.
A short body is easier to scan than a paragraph.
Use min-height on the action so it has a comfortable hit area.
Publish after saving and confirm the card appears in the gallery.

lessons.takeaway: Know which Keystone surface you are extending before you write the component; the Admin UI and the public showcase have different jobs.

knowledge_check.question: Which API does a public Keystone frontend normally use to read content?
knowledge_check.explanation: Keystone generates a GraphQL API from your list schema. Public surfaces query that API, not Prisma or the database file directly.

deep_dive.title: Admin vs public
deep_dive.body: Custom admin pages live under admin/pages and are part of Keystone’s Admin UI. The public showcase is a separate React surface that queries Keystone through GraphQL. They can share a design language, but they do not share a runtime.

deep_dive.title: The GraphQL boundary
deep_dive.body: Keystone generates queries and mutations from your list schema. The public showcase and the Lumina lab read and write through that API, not through Prisma directly.

deep_dive.title: Component boundaries
deep_dive.body: Keep data fetching at the page boundary. Move interactivity into small client components so the showcase and the live preview stay predictable.

lessons.title: Design tokens as data
lessons.outcome: Model a small token contract in Keystone and render every component from the same variables.
mental_model: **Tokens are the contract.** Color, radius, spacing, type scale, and elevation are data, not one-off styles.
**Keystone stores the values; CSS variables carry them.** The token list holds the source values, and the component writes them into `:root` before it renders.
**Theme is a token, not a second stylesheet.** A light/dark switch changes values, not every component.

lab.title: Tune a token-driven button
lab.brief: Build the primary action with CSS custom properties. The same button should cover default, hover, active, focus-visible, disabled, and busy states.
checklist: At least 44px tall
Hover and active feedback
Visible focus-visible ring
Disabled state is readable
Accent and text pass contrast
hints: Use spacing to reach the hit area instead of a larger font.
Declare the token contract on :root, then consume it with var().
A ghost button needs a visible boundary on focus.
Set aria-busy while the action is running so the state is announced.

lessons.takeaway: A small, explicit token contract keeps every component consistent without duplicating CSS.

knowledge_check.question: Why store design tokens in Keystone instead of hard-coding them in each component?
options: It makes the components render faster
It gives every component one source of truth for visual decisions
It removes the need for CSS
knowledge_check.explanation: Tokens create a shared contract. Changing a value in Keystone updates every component that consumes the same variables, while contrast still needs to be tested.

deep_dive.title: The token contract
deep_dive.body: Start with the decisions every component shares: accent, background, foreground, muted text, radius, spacing, type scale, and shadow. Add more only when a real component needs them.

deep_dive.title: Token storage
deep_dive.body: Keystone can store the token object in a json field or a dedicated token list. Keep the shape small and stable, validate it at the edge, and expose it to components as CSS variables.

deep_dive.title: Contrast is not automatic
deep_dive.body: A beautiful accent can still fail contrast. Check text on the background and the action label on the accent; aim for 4.5:1 for body text and 3:1 for large text and UI boundaries.

lessons.title: Accessible primitives
lessons.outcome: Build a form that works with a keyboard, a screen reader, and a thumb.
mental_model: **Labels are part of the control.** A placeholder is an example, not a label.
**Focus is a state.** `:focus-visible` tells keyboard users where they are without flashing a ring on every click.
**Feedback closes the loop.** A success or error message must be text, associated with the field, and announced.

lab.title: Build the contact form
lab.brief: Add visible labels, the right input types, required fields, and a success message that does not reload the page. Test the form with the keyboard.
checklist: Every field has a visible label
Email uses type=email
Required fields are marked
Submit shows a success message
Keyboard focus is visible
hints: Connect each label with for and id.
Use autocomplete=name and autocomplete=email.
role="status" announces the success message without stealing focus.
Keep the form markup semantic: form, label, input, textarea, button.

lessons.takeaway: Accessibility is not a final pass; it is the shape of the primitive itself.

knowledge_check.question: Which attributes connect a label to an input?
knowledge_check.explanation: The label's for attribute must match the input's id. Clicking the label then focuses the input, and screen readers announce them together.

deep_dive.title: Labels vs placeholders
deep_dive.body: A placeholder disappears after typing and cannot be relied on as a label. Keep a visible label above the field and use the placeholder for an example.

deep_dive.title: Focus-visible
deep_dive.body: Use `:focus-visible` for the keyboard ring. It keeps the pointer experience clean while giving keyboard users a clear target. Never remove focus outlines without a replacement.

deep_dive.title: Status messages
deep_dive.body: A `role="status"` element announces polite updates such as “Message sent.” For errors, associate the message with the field and mark the field invalid.

lessons.title: Custom admin components
lessons.outcome: Replace a piece of the Keystone Admin UI with your own React component and keep access control intact.
mental_model: **admin/pages is the extension point.** Custom pages are React routes inside Keystone’s Admin UI.
**Access is part of the page.** Keystone’s `isAccessAllowed` and list access control decide who can see the page and the data.
**Keep the admin’s job small.** A dashboard card should answer one question and link to the collection behind it.

lab.title: Build a dashboard stat card
lab.brief: Design a small card for the Keystone dashboard. It should answer one question and link to the collection behind it. This lab is a visual prototype: real Keystone admin views are React components.
checklist: One number is the focus
The trend explains the number
The footnote adds context
It fits the admin's dark theme
No action is hidden behind a hover
hints: Use the accent for the trend, not the whole card.
Keep the label and footnote quiet.
A dashboard card should be readable at a glance.
The link is part of the card; make it visible without hovering.

lessons.takeaway: Admin customization is real application code: keep it small, access-aware, and focused on the editor’s job.

knowledge_check.question: Where do you add a custom Keystone Admin UI page?
knowledge_check.explanation: Files in `admin/pages` become routes in Keystone’s Admin UI. The default export is the page component; `admin/config.ts` controls navigation and branding.

deep_dive.title: Custom admin pages
deep_dive.body: Files in `admin/pages` become routes in the Admin UI. The default export is the page component; use `admin/config.ts` for navigation and the logo.

deep_dive.title: Access still applies
deep_dive.body: `ui.isAccessAllowed` controls the Admin UI, but list access control still protects the data. Use both; hiding a page is not authorization.

deep_dive.title: Custom navigation
deep_dive.body: A custom Navigation component can link to your dashboard, the public showcase, and the lists that matter. Keep the editor’s path short.

lessons.title: Custom field components
lessons.outcome: Build a field view that reads and writes a Keystone JSON value without breaking the Admin UI contract.
mental_model: **A field view has a controller and React views.** The controller selects and serializes the value; the Field renders the editor.
**`ui.views` points at your module.** A JSON field can be upgraded with a color swatch, helper text, and a picker.
**Validation and access stay at the schema boundary.** A custom view improves the editor; it does not replace field access or validation.

lab.title: Build a color token field
lab.brief: Create the field an editor uses to set the accent token. It needs a swatch, a hex value, a helper line, and a live preview. Real Keystone field components are React; this lab prototypes the control.
checklist: The control has a visible label
A swatch and hex value stay in sync
Helper text explains where the token is used
The control is keyboard reachable
The value is valid before save
hints: Use type=color for the picker and a text input for the hex value.
Validate with a hex pattern before updating the preview.
The helper text is part of the field, not decoration.
Use aria-invalid and a status message for invalid input.

starter.html: Used for primary actions and focus rings.

solution.html: Used for primary actions and focus rings.

lessons.takeaway: A custom field view is a form control with a contract: read the value, emit the change, and leave authorization to Keystone.

knowledge_check.question: Which option registers a custom field view on a Keystone JSON field?
knowledge_check.explanation: `ui.views` is resolved as a module path. The module exports the controller and the React views that replace the default JSON editor.

deep_dive.title: Controller and views
deep_dive.body: The controller maps the GraphQL selection, deserializes the stored value, and serializes edits. The Field component renders the editable control; the Cell renders the list column.

deep_dive.title: JSON fields
deep_dive.body: A json field is a good home for a small, well-known value such as a color token. Validate the shape in the view and keep the schema simple.

deep_dive.title: Access vs validation
deep_dive.body: Field access decides who can read or update the value. Validation decides whether the value is acceptable. A custom view does not replace either.

lessons.title: Blocks and the page builder
lessons.outcome: Model a page as reusable JSON blocks and render it with a one-to-one React registry.
mental_model: **Blocks are typed rows.** Each block has a `blockType` and its own fields; the array preserves order.
**One block, one renderer.** A registry maps `blockType` to a component, so adding a block is a schema change plus a renderer.
**Structure stays in Keystone.** Editors compose and reorder; developers keep the rendering predictable.

lab.title: Compose a page from blocks
lab.brief: Build a page from distinct sections: a hero, a feature grid, a testimonial, and a call to action. Each block should stand on its own and survive a narrow screen.
checklist: Each block has a clear purpose
The page follows a readable order
The feature grid wraps at 360px
The call to action is obvious
Every section has semantic markup
hints: Use section elements with aria-labelledby for each block.
A feature grid can be one rule: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(180px, 1fr)).
Keep one block, one visual idea.
Publish after saving and check the page preview in the showcase.

lessons.takeaway: Blocks turn a page into a small, typed component system that editors can compose without breaking the design.

knowledge_check.question: What identifies which renderer a saved block uses?
knowledge_check.explanation: Keystone stores `blockType` with each block. The renderer looks up that value to choose the React component.

deep_dive.title: Block storage
deep_dive.body: Keystone stores the block array in a json field. Validate the array shape and keep a small set of block types.

deep_dive.title: Validation
deep_dive.body: Check required fields and maximum block counts before publish. A page builder without guardrails becomes a layout lottery.

deep_dive.title: Rendering
deep_dive.body: A registry keyed by `blockType` is enough for most teams. Unknown blocks should render nothing or a safe fallback, never crash the page.

lessons.outcome: Design a Keystone relationship field view that makes linked items, cardinality, and the create-or-connect choice clear.
mental_model: **Relationships encode cardinality.** The UI should make one versus many visible before an editor changes the field.
**Linked items are navigation.** A relationship summary should help editors inspect the connected item without losing the current form.
**Create and connect are different intents.** Give each action a distinct label and consequence.

lessons.outcome: Build a Keystone list filter bar that exposes query constraints, active filters, and a fast way to clear the current result set.
mental_model: **Filters are query state.** The UI should show which constraints are currently shaping the list.
**A filter needs an exit.** Clear one filter or reset all without forcing editors to reload the page.
**The empty result is part of the control.** Explain when a query returns nothing and how to recover.

deep_dive.title: List queries
deep_dive.body: Keystone list queries should request the fields the card needs and apply access control before content reaches the public component.

deep_dive.title: Shareable state
deep_dive.body: For production filters, mirror the selection in the URL so a filtered resource view can be bookmarked or shared.

deep_dive.title: Empty results
deep_dive.body: A useful empty state distinguishes no content from a filter that intentionally narrowed the result set.

lessons.title: Design a GraphQL query state
lessons.outcome: Give a Keystone GraphQL-powered view clear loading, error, and retry states without hiding the query boundary.
mental_model: **Loading, error, and empty are different states.** Each one needs different copy and a different next action.
**The query boundary is part of UX.** Tell users what the screen is waiting for and what retry will do.
**Errors should recover.** Preserve the view context and offer retry instead of replacing the page with a stack trace.

Retry button is keyboard accessible

Empty content is not called an error
hints: Use role=status for polite loading updates.
Error copy should say what the user can try next.
Do not show a generic empty message when the query failed.

lessons.takeaway: A GraphQL query is only finished when its loading, error, retry, and empty states help the user recover.

knowledge_check.question: Why should a failed query not render the empty state?
options: It hides the difference between no data and a request failure
knowledge_check.explanation: No data and a failed request have different causes and different recovery actions.

deep_dive.title: GraphQL errors
deep_dive.body: A GraphQL response can contain data and errors together. Decide which partial data is safe to show and communicate degraded results.

deep_dive.title: Retry policy
deep_dive.body: Retry transient failures, but avoid an endless loop. A user-triggered retry gives control and makes the action observable.

deep_dive.title: Server and client
deep_dive.body: Fetch public content on the server when possible, then keep retry and interaction behavior in a small client component.

lessons.title: Build a Keystone area chart
lessons.outcome: Build a responsive Keystone area chart that reveals the volume and direction of GraphQL-backed content activity without hiding the values behind decoration.
mental_model: **Filled space shows volume.** An area chart makes accumulated movement feel tangible across an ordered Keystone sequence.
**The row is the contract.** Labels, values, and units stay editable so the chart is never disconnected from GraphQL content.
**Responsive is a reading order.** Keep the baseline, peaks, and summary available as the card narrows.

The filled area reflects edited values immediately
Peaks and slowdowns work without hover
Labels and units survive narrow layouts

lessons.takeaway: A Keystone area chart is a view over an ordered query result: the baseline, filled volume, and responsive labels must agree.

knowledge_check.question: What does the filled area emphasize?
options: The volume and direction of an ordered series
The number of pixels in the card
knowledge_check.explanation: The area connects ordered values and uses filled space to make volume, peaks, and slowdowns easier to perceive.

deep_dive.title: Baseline and volume
deep_dive.body: The area fill should support the line, not obscure it. A clear baseline helps learners read both direction and relative volume.

deep_dive.title: Mobile hierarchy
deep_dive.body: On a narrow screen, preserve the title, unit, baseline, and strongest peak. Short labels prevent the chart from becoming a horizontal scroll problem.

deep_dive.title: GraphQL contract
deep_dive.body: Keystone can return structured activity rows while the area renderer chooses the visual treatment. The saved values remain independent of the SVG.

lessons.title: Build a Keystone radar chart
lessons.outcome: Create a responsive Keystone radar chart that compares the shape of moderation dimensions and keeps the summary useful without hover.
mental_model: **Axes create meaning.** A radar chart compares several dimensions around one center, so each label needs a stable definition.
**The shape is a profile.** The polygon shows balance and gaps between moderation dimensions, while values keep it precise.
**Responsive is not smaller desktop.** The radar can resize while axis labels and the numeric context preserve the message.

lab.title: Profile moderation dimensions
lab.brief: Edit Keystone moderation dimensions, tune the radar presentation, and test whether the profile and labels stay clear at different widths.
checklist: Each axis represents a distinct dimension
The profile updates from the rows
A strength or gap is easy to locate
Labels and values remain available without hover
The customized profile data is saved in Keystone

content.title: Items moderated
content.caption: A Keystone moderation queue across one working week.

hints: Use dimension labels that make the axes meaningful.
Lower one value and ask whether the profile gap is obvious.
Keep numeric values visible so the insight is not trapped in the SVG.

lessons.takeaway: A Keystone radar chart should expose the balance of a moderation profile while preserving the dimensions and values that give it meaning.

knowledge_check.question: What makes a Keystone radar chart trustworthy?
options: Stable axis meanings and readable value summaries
A tooltip that only appears on hover
knowledge_check.explanation: A radar profile only communicates clearly when every axis has a stable meaning and its values remain available in text.

deep_dive.title: Stable axes
deep_dive.body: Radar charts compare dimensions, not time. Keep the same axis meanings and order so profiles can be interpreted consistently.

deep_dive.title: Accessible profile
deep_dive.body: Keep dimension labels and exact values in text so the profile survives without pointer hover, fine-grained SVG inspection, or color perception.

deep_dive.title: Responsive polygon
deep_dive.body: A responsive radar changes its available size, not the underlying profile. The normalized rows remain the source of truth.

lessons.title: Drafts, preview, publish
lessons.outcome: Move a component from draft to published, preview it before the public sees it, and make the state visible.
mental_model: **Draft and published are states.** Keystone stores `status` on the component; the public filter only returns published, public rows.
**Preview is the same document.** The editor and the public showcase both render the saved HTML/CSS/JS in a sandboxed frame, so what learners see is what ships.
**Access control is the door.** Public reads must exclude drafts; the UI should never be the only thing hiding them.

lab.title: Draft, preview, and publish a pricing table
lab.brief: Build a three-plan pricing table, save it as a draft, inspect it in the preview, then publish it to the showcase. The billing toggle should stay understandable at every width.
checklist: Three plans share one card structure
The recommended plan is obvious without relying on color alone
Prices stay readable at 360px
The billing toggle is keyboard accessible
The published version appears in the showcase
hints: Keep the plan markup identical; use a modifier class for the featured plan.
Use grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(220px, 1fr)).
Save first; then publish the version you want the public to see.
Open the showcase after publishing and confirm the card appears.

lessons.takeaway: Publishing is a workflow, not a button: save the draft, preview the real component, then flip the public state.

knowledge_check.question: What keeps draft components out of public Keystone GraphQL queries?
options: A public access filter on status and surface
knowledge_check.explanation: Keystone list access can return a filter for unauthenticated queries. The filter must exclude drafts and admin-surface components; the UI is not the security boundary.

deep_dive.title: Status and access
deep_dive.body: Keystone list access can return a filter for unauthenticated queries. Keep drafts and admin-surface components out of that filter.

deep_dive.title: Preview
deep_dive.body: The editor preview and the public showcase render the same saved document. Check the published version in the showcase before you call it done.

deep_dive.title: The access boundary
deep_dive.body: Hiding a draft in the UI is not security. The GraphQL access filter must exclude it.

lessons.title: Capstone: the showcase
lessons.outcome: Ship a polished testimonial to the public showcase and verify it survives every device and state.
mental_model: **The showcase is a product surface.** It has a hierarchy, a filter model, and a quality bar; it is not a debug page.
**Polish is systems work.** Responsive layout, contrast, focus, and empty states are part of the component, not a final coat of paint.
**Publishing is a promise.** Once a component is public, it represents the course; check it before you flip the state.

lab.title: Publish your capstone testimonial
lab.brief: Build the testimonial you want in the showcase. Make the quote, author, company, and rating readable, then publish the final version.
checklist: The quote is the first thing you read
The author and company are easy to find
The rating has a text alternative
It reads well at 360px
The published version appears in the showcase
hints: Use blockquote and figcaption, not div soup.
Give the stars an aria-label instead of relying on color.
Test the card at 360px before publishing.
Open the showcase after publishing and confirm the card appears.

lessons.takeaway: A component is finished when it holds up in the showcase, on a phone, with a keyboard, in both themes.

knowledge_check.question: Which check belongs before publishing a component to the showcase?
options: The component has a unique animation
The layout survives mobile and contrast passes
The name is longer than the description
knowledge_check.explanation: Publishing is a quality gate. Responsive behavior and contrast are baseline checks; decoration is optional.

deep_dive.title: Responsive by construction
deep_dive.body: Use fluid widths, `minmax`, and wrapping instead of fixed pixel layouts. Test the component at 360px, 768px, and full width before publishing.

deep_dive.title: Content quality
deep_dive.body: A showcase is only as good as its weakest entry. Complete attributions, specific copy, and one clear idea per component make the gallery useful to the next learner.

deep_dive.title: Moderation
deep_dive.body: Learner-published does not mean unmoderated. The admin can feature, unpublish, or delete a submission; the public GraphQL filter only ever exposes published, public components.

lessons.title: Build a numeric data table
lessons.outcome: Create a small table of numbers, style it with the shared build controls, save it to Keystone, and read the same rows in the Level 8 chart.
mental_model: **The form is the schema.** Title, caption, unit, and rows are the data contract the chart reads.
**Reuse the controls.** The same BuilderFields inputs and design tokens drive the form and the live table.
**Save, then fetch.** The table is stored in the CMS; Level 8 loads the newest saved table and turns it into a bar chart.
**Keep it small.** A short numeric table is easy to validate, reload, and chart.

lab.title: Save a table of numbers
lab.brief: Edit the rows and labels, adjust the design tokens, then save the table to Keystone. The newest saved table becomes the saved-form chart in the Level 8 showcase.
checklist: Every row has a label and a number
The table title describes the data
The unit is visible
The design tokens still pass contrast
The table is saved in the CMS

content.title: Support tickets by category
content.caption: A small numeric table saved in Keystone and reused by the Level 8 chart.

hints: Use the Number rows list to add, remove, or reorder rows.
The chart uses the row labels as categories and the values as bars.
Save again to update the same table, or reset to start a new version.

lessons.takeaway: A small, validated table saved in Keystone is enough data to drive a real chart without exposing the CMS credentials.

knowledge_check.question: Where should the Level 8 chart get the numbers from the form?
options: From the newest saved data-table component in Keystone
From a hard-coded array in the chart component
From the browser's local storage only
knowledge_check.explanation: The form saves its rows in Keystone. The Level 8 server loader reads the newest saved table, validates the rows, and passes a small chart-ready series to the browser.

deep_dive.title: Why store rows, not markup?
deep_dive.body: The builder saves the labels and numbers as structured content. The preview can change without losing the data, and the chart reads the same values instead of scraping the table.

deep_dive.title: One contract, two views
deep_dive.body: The form preview and the Level 8 chart both consume the same title, unit, and row objects. That keeps the data honest when either view changes.

deep_dive.title: Small data is still data
deep_dive.body: Validation belongs at the edge: require labels, finite numbers, and a bounded row count so a malformed table cannot break the chart.

lessons.title: Build a responsive analytics summary
lessons.outcome: Compose a Keystone analytics summary that keeps metrics, comparison text, and responsive layout readable at every width.
mental_model: **Metrics need a comparison.** A number without a period or baseline is not an insight.
**Responsive data has a reading order.** Keep the primary metric first and let supporting cards wrap below it.
**Summary text is a fallback.** The key change should survive if a visual chart or hover interaction is unavailable.

lab.title: Compose the analytics summary
lab.brief: Build a responsive summary from Keystone aggregates. Make the total, period, and comparison readable without relying on a chart.
checklist: Primary metric has a period label
Comparison is written in text
Cards wrap below 560px
Decorative icon is hidden from assistive technology
Summary remains useful without hover
hints: Use a heading and a supporting period together.
Say “up 12% from last week” instead of only coloring the number green.
Use CSS grid with minmax for responsive cards.

lessons.takeaway: A responsive analytics summary turns Keystone aggregates into a readable decision surface before any chart is drawn.

knowledge_check.question: What should accompany a headline metric?
knowledge_check.explanation: Period and comparison context make the metric interpretable and useful.

deep_dive.title: Aggregate contracts
deep_dive.body: Define the metric payload before styling: value, period, comparison, and label. This keeps the UI independent from database details.

deep_dive.title: Responsive priority
deep_dive.body: At narrow widths, stack secondary metrics below the primary one instead of shrinking every value until it becomes hard to scan.

deep_dive.title: Accessible summaries
deep_dive.body: Textual comparisons make the insight available without color, hover, motion, or a particular chart library.
